\chapter{Green and Yellow}
\label{ch:ka-green-and-yellow}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name green and yellow in Kannada, on top of the four colours I already had.}

Say \kn{ಹಸಿರು}, a true cousin of Tamil paccai and Telugu pacca, then \kn{ಹಳದಿ}, the turmeric-borrowing that is secretly a cousin of German gelb.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[\kn{ಹಸಿರು}, \kn{ಹಳದಿ}]{\kn{ಹಸಿರು}, \kn{ಹಳದಿ} — a real Dravidian family, and a borrowed cousin of gelb}

\label{lesson:KA-C22-hasiru-haladi}



\begin{quote}
Kannada's green word belongs to a real Dravidian family you'll meet again soon. Its yellow word isn't native at all — and it turns out to be hiding the very same ancient root this whole arc keeps circling back to.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\kn{ಹಸಿರು}} (\textbf{hasiru}, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{green}\textquotedblright{}) comes from \textbf{Old Kannada} \textbf{\kn{ಪಸಿರ್}} (\textbf{pasir}), from \textbf{Proto-Dravidian} \emph{\textbf{*pac-}}, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{green}\textquotedblright{} — the \textbf{exact same root} behind \textbf{Tamil}'s \textbf{\ta{பச்சை}} (\emph{paccai}) and \textbf{Telugu}'s \textbf{\te{పచ్చ}} (\emph{pacca}). Kannada even keeps a doublet of its own, \textbf{\kn{ಪಚ್ಚೆ}} (\emph{pacce}), sitting right alongside \emph{hasiru}. So unlike Kannada's \textbf{blue} (\kn{ನೀಲಿ}, borrowed from Sanskrit), green here is the real, deep, native Dravidian word — and this particular root will keep resurfacing as Telugu, Malayalam, and Tamil's own green words come up later in this same arc.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\kn{ಹಳದಿ}} (\textbf{haḷadi}, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{yellow}\textquotedblright{}) is \textbf{not} Kannada's native turmeric word — that's \textbf{\kn{ಅರಿಶಿನ}} (\emph{ariśina}). Instead, \emph{haḷadi} appears to be shaped by Sanskrit/Hindi \textbf{\dv{हरिद्रा}/\dv{हल्दी}} (\textbf{haridrā}/\emph{haldi}, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{turmeric}\textquotedblright{}), the same word that gives \textquotedblleft{}turmeric\textquotedblright{} across a huge swath of Indo-Aryan languages (Hindi/Urdu/Punjabi \emph{haldi}, Bengali \emph{holud}, Odia \emph{haladi}) — and in some of these, like Bengali and Odia, that turmeric-word doubles as the everyday word for the color \textbf{yellow} itself, exactly as \emph{haḷadi} does in Kannada (Hindi keeps the two separate: \emph{haldi} stays \textquotedblleft{}turmeric,\textquotedblright{} while \textquotedblleft{}yellow\textquotedblright{} is the unrelated word \emph{pīlā}). Here's the part that closes a loop running through this whole arc: \textbf{haridrā} itself traces back to \textbf{\dv{हरि}} (\textbf{hari}, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{yellow, tawny}\textquotedblright{}), from \textbf{Proto-Indo- European} \emph{\textbf{*ǵ\textsuperscript{h}elh\textsubscript{3}-}} — the \textbf{same ancient root} already behind Hindi's own \textbf{\dv{हरा}} (\emph{harā}, \textquotedblleft{}green\textquotedblright{}) and German's \textbf{gelb} (\textquotedblleft{}yellow\textquotedblright{}). So Kannada picked up its yellow word from a completely different language family, Indo-Aryan rather than Dravidian — and that borrowed word still lands on the exact same PIE root this arc has been tracing all along.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\kn{ಹಸಿರು}\textquotedblright{} — green, a real Dravidian cousin of Tamil paccai and Telugu pacca
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\kn{ಹಳದಿ}\textquotedblright{} — yellow, borrowed, and secretly a cousin of gelb
  \item the contrast — hasiru is native Dravidian; haladi is a Sanskrit/ Hindi loan built on the turmeric word
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What Proto-Dravidian root gives \textbf{\kn{ಹಸಿರು}} (\emph{hasiru}), and which two other Dravidian languages share it? (\emph{\textbf{*pac-}}, \textquotedblleft{}green\textquotedblright{} — shared with \textbf{Tamil}'s \emph{paccai} and \textbf{Telugu}'s \emph{pacca}.) Is \textbf{\kn{ಹಳದಿ}} (\emph{haḷadi}) Kannada's native word for turmeric? (\textbf{No} — that's \emph{ariśina}; \emph{haḷadi} is a Sanskrit/Hindi loan.) What ancient PIE root connects \textbf{haḷadi}, through Sanskrit \textbf{hari}, to Hindi's \textbf{harā} and German's \textbf{gelb}? (\emph{\textbf{*ǵ\textsuperscript{h}elh\textsubscript{3}-}}, \textquotedblleft{}to shine.\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
